conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: FirstHourFavorableEntryWindow
candidates.quote: There is a tendency for the first hour or two to be the most likely time of the day to find a trade where you can make two to three times your risk... most traders should work very hard to take trades in the first hour or two.
candidates.description: Restrict or favor entries to the first N hours of the trading session (the exchange clock's close time), when the reward:risk:probability combination is best.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: a fixed clock-time window test, same shape as the existing TimeWindow rule

notes: Session open time (630 = 6:30 a.m. PST) is illustrative for the Emini; instrument-specific.

candidates.name: MidDayLowProbabilityWindowFilter
candidates.quote: The middle of the day, beginning around 8:30 to 9:30 a.m. PST and ending around 11:00 to 11:30 and sometimes as late as 12:30, is more prone to two-sided trading... Beginning traders tend to lose money in the middle third of the day... they should consider not trading in the middle third unless signals are especially strong.
candidates.description: Block or restrict ordinary stop-entries during the mid-session window (roughly 8:30/9:30-11:00/12:30 PST), which tends to be two-sided, range-bound, and lower win rate.

complexity.reason: a fixed clock-time window test, applied negated ahead of other entries

notes: Brooks's carve-out ('unless signals are especially strong') is left as a design decision for the authoring pass - not mechanized here.

candidates.name: MidDayFadeWeakSignalBarAtRangeExtreme
candidates.quote: Experienced traders will sell on limit orders above weak high 1 and high 2 buy signal bars at the top, and buy on limit orders below weak low 1 and low 2 signal bars at the bottom.
candidates.description: During the mid-session two-sided window, fade a weak high1/high2 buy signal bar at the top of the range (sell on a limit order above it) or a weak low1/low2 sell signal bar at the bottom (buy below it) - a countertrend scalp against the existing high1/high2/low1/low2 setups.
candidates.pseudocode: isMiddaySession && weakHigh1Or2SignalBar[0] && high[0] >= rangeTop - toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: sell/buy on a LIMIT order above/below the weak signal bar, not a stop entry - the opposite mechanization convention from the rest of the corpus

complexity.reason: combines existing high1/high2/low1/low2 primitives, a 'weak signal bar' quality judgment, a trading-range-top/bottom test, and a limit-order (not stop) entry mechanism

notes: Depends on the High1/High2/Low1/Low2 primitives already defined in earlier chapters; not redefined here.

candidates.name: MiddayReversalTimeWindow
candidates.quote: The market often reverses around 8:30 a.m. PST and then trends for the rest of the middle third of the day.
candidates.description: There is an elevated chance of at least a partial reversal or a decisive re-assessment of the day's direction around a specific clock time (~8:30 a.m. PST); use as a time gate on reversal-pattern entries.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (time gate on other reversal-pattern entries)
notes: Brooks describes this as a tendency, not a certainty; the actual reversal-pattern test it gates is defined elsewhere.

candidates.name: FinalHourTrendContinuationNoPullbackEntry
candidates.quote: Traders who want to enter on pullbacks get trapped out because a pullback never comes. If you see this, enter with the trend on the close of the current bar and put your protective stop beyond the other end of the bar.
candidates.description: In the final 30-60 minutes of the session, when a strong trend keeps making new closes in the trend direction without a pullback, enter with the trend at the close of the current bar (rather than waiting for a pullback), stop beyond the bar's opposite extreme.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.Time() >= finalPeriodStart && close[0] > close[1] && close[1] > close[2]
candidates.book_order_type: buy/sell at the close of the current bar (market), protective stop beyond the low/high of that same bar

complexity.reason: combines a fixed time window with a short run of consecutive same-direction closes as the 'no pullback' momentum test

notes: finalPeriodStart illustrated at 12:30 PST (final 30-60 minutes before the Emini's 1:00 p.m. PST close); the 'no pullback' test (two consecutive same-direction closes) is a reading, Brooks gives no precise count.

candidates.name: DailyTrendBiasFinalHourContinuation
candidates.quote: When there is a bull trend on the daily chart, there will almost always be more bull trend bars than bear trend bars... experienced traders will be quick to short any rally that begins to reverse down toward the end of the day [of a bear-trend day], expecting a close near the low of the day.
candidates.description: In the final 30-60 minutes, bias with-trend entries toward the prevailing daily-chart trend direction (buy pullbacks in a daily bull trend / sell rallies in a daily bear trend), expecting the day to close near its high/low.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter biasing which with-trend entries to take)

complexity.reason: requires a higher-timeframe (daily) trend-context read alongside the intraday final-hour time window

notes: dailyBullTrendContext is the daily-chart trend-context primitive defined elsewhere (research-grade itself); not redefined here.

candidates.name: AlwaysInTrendTradeAfterEstablished
candidates.quote: Once the always-in direction has been established, then look to take the trend trade. Even though you might miss the first bar or two, if the trend is strong, there will be plenty of points left in the trade.
candidates.description: Once the always-in direction for the day has been established, take with-trend entries even after missing the earliest bars of the move.
candidates.pseudocode: // depends on the always-in primitive, itself flagged research-grade (Chapter 15, 'Always In')

complexity.reason: depends entirely on the always-in-direction concept, which the mining brief itself names as a research-grade design decision

notes: 'Always in' is defined in this book's Chapter 15; not redefined here.

candidates.name: FinalHourChoppyTrendWideStopHold
candidates.quote: The market will trend into the close but have large bars, big tails, and two or three reversals that run stops but do not hit the original stop beyond the signal bar... swing the trade and stick to your initial stop until after the pullback, and then tighten your stop to just beyond the pullback.
candidates.description: In the final 30-60 minutes, when a with-trend position is open and the market is choppy (large tails, repeated stop-running reversals) but has not yet hit the original stop beyond the signal bar, keep the wide initial stop rather than tightening prematurely; only tighten once the pullback has clearly ended.
candidates.pseudocode: // 'large tails' and 'two or three reversals' are not precisely quantified by Brooks; a design decision is needed on the pullback-end test before this can be coded exactly
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (stop-management guidance, not a new order)

complexity.reason: requires defining 'choppy with large tails' and 'the pullback has ended' as precise bar-level tests

rejected.quote: Whenever a report is released, whether it is a 7 a.m. PST housing report or an 11:15 a.m. FOMC announcement, slippage is common... most traders should wait for seconds to minutes until the market becomes orderly before placing a trade.
rejected.reason: requires an economic calendar / scheduled news-release times, data the engine does not have beyond bar prices and the clock

rejected.quote: Computers have a clear edge in speed of analysis and order placement, and they are your competitors. When your competition has a big advantage, don't compete.
rejected.reason: pure discretion/philosophy about competing with algorithmic traders, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Since the high or low of the day forms during the first third of the day in maybe 90 percent of days...
rejected.reason: a descriptive statistic used to justify other heuristics, not itself an if-then bar-level condition

rejected.quote: Beginning traders... often lose more than they have made in the first third of the day, and if that is the case, they should consider not trading in the middle third
rejected.reason: requires the individual trader's own historical performance broken out by time of day, which is personal trading-record data outside OHLCV/position-state

chapter_summary: Chapter 11 splits the trading day into three periods and gives generalizations for each: the first hour or two has the best reward:risk:probability and deserves the most effort; the middle third (roughly 8:30/9:30 to 11:00/12:30 PST) is prone to two-sided, range-bound trading where stop entries do poorly and fading weak high1/high2/low1/low2 signals with limit orders does better, with an inflection often near 8:30 a.m.; and the final 30-60 minutes often either resumes or reverses the day's trend, sometimes relentlessly (driven by risk-manager and momentum-program covering) and sometimes choppily with large tails. All candidates here are intraday-only and mostly time-window filters (several likely duplicate the existing TimeWindow rule) composed with momentum/trend-context primitives defined elsewhere; the always-in and daily-trend-bias ideas are flagged research/hard pending those primitives' own designs.
